supplement.where: Supplementary material referred to on p. 4, Section 3.3.3 ("the full codebook is in the supplementary material"); no URL given
supplement.holds: The full codebook for coding added, edited, and deleted ideas. Appendices A to G (design brief, expert table, system prompt, researcher manual, guidance prompts, post-survey items, qualitative themes) are in this PDF.

paper_design_summary: Forty-five design students did an online (Zoom) interaction-design task: redesign a city 311 non-emergency reporting website on a Miro board over two iterations. Between iterations each student was randomly assigned to one of three 15-minute conditions: Self Reflection (unsupported review), Stepwise Guidance (written prompts on constructive conflict), or Interactive Engagement (a GPT-4.1 agent that posts stakeholder pushback points on the student's proposal). The first author coded ideas added, edited, and deleted between iterations, and all students completed a 7-point post-survey; no rater scored the creativity or novelty of the proposals.

assignment.what_was_assigned: The intervention given between design iteration 1 and design iteration 2: Self Reflection, Stepwise Guidance, or Interactive Engagement with the antagonistic AI agent
assignment.quote: We recruited 45 design students from Design and Information Science departments, with each randomly assigned to one of the three groups.

arms.name: Self Reflection
arms.description: Reviewed and reflected on their own design proposal for about 12 minutes without editing, then thought aloud for about 3 minutes

arms.name: Stepwise Guidance
arms.description: Read a written stepwise introduction to constructive conflict, adapted from the agent's system prompt, and thought aloud

arms.name: Interactive Engagement
arms.description: Saw four agent-generated stakeholder pushback points, tagged and steered them, then saw a second set of four points

participants.who: Design students from Design and Information Science departments; mean age 25.08 (SD 3.68), on average 4 years of studying design/HCI (SD 1.79; PDF p. 4, Section 3.3.2). Stepwise Guidance has an explicit analyzed-group denominator of 15 in the stakeholder analysis (accessibility 7/15 and privacy 7/15; PDF p. 6, Section 4.2.1). Interactive Engagement has an explicit denominator of 15 in "14 of 15 participants used these features" (PDF p. 7, Section 4.3.1). No separate Self Reflection arm total or per-arm randomized counts are explicitly printed; these remain null. The paper reports 45 design proposals and 90 iterations analyzed (PDF p. 5, Sections 3.4-3.4.1). No exclusions are reported.
participants.quote: We recruited 45 design students from Design and Information Science departments, with each randomly assigned to one of the three groups.
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 3.3.2; p. 5, Section 3.4 ("From the study, we collected 45 design proposals, 90 iterations")

ai_tool.name_model: Antagonistic stakeholder-pushback agent built in Miro; GPT-4.1 generates critique points (GPT-4o parses visual content, Whisper processes voice input)
ai_tool.how_used: The agent read the student's first-iteration proposal and generated two rounds of four stakeholder pushback points as sticky notes; the student tagged points (useful, not useful, custom) and could use Consensus and Command frames to steer the second round. A researcher triggered the sends with fixed triggers (wizard-assisted).

task.description: Interaction design proposal for redesigning a local government non-emergency civic reporting (311) website, written as sticky notes on a Miro board, in two iterations
task.duration: About 90 minutes in total: iteration 1 20-30 minutes, condition phase 15 minutes, iteration 2 15-25 minutes

outcomes.name: Ideas added in the second iteration
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct new idea units added to the second proposal iteration, identified from sticky notes and checked against think-aloud and walkthrough evidence (PDF p. 4, Section 3.3.3; p. 5, Sections 3.4.1 and 4.1.1). This is output-coded fluency. Source discrepancy: Figure 2, right panel, labels the mean addition segments 2.4 for Self Reflection and 0.9 for Stepwise Guidance, whereas Section 4.1.1 prints 2.13 and 0.80, respectively. The reported statistics retain the results-text values; the paper does not explain the discrepancy (PDF p. 5).

contrasts.reported: Kruskal-Wallis H(2) = 9.12, p = .010, epsilon^2 = .21. Self Reflection M = 2.13, SD = 1.36; Stepwise Guidance M = 0.80, SD = 1.15 (vs Self Reflection p_adj = .008, Hedges' g = -1.03); Interactive Engagement M = 1.27, SD = 0.80 (vs Self Reflection p_adj = .446; vs Stepwise Guidance p_adj = .346)

outcomes.name: Ideas edited between iterations (revisions plus enhancements)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Ideas coded as edited between iterations, comprising revisions (partial deletion and restart) and enhancements (redevelopment of an existing idea; PDF p. 4, Section 3.3.3). Enhancements: Stepwise Guidance versus Self Reflection p_adj = .036; Interactive Engagement versus Self Reflection p_adj = .030; Guidance versus Engagement was not significant. Revisions: Interactive Engagement versus Self Reflection p_adj = .023; Guidance versus Self Reflection was not significant. Five Interactive Engagement participants revised six ideas; one Stepwise Guidance participant revised one idea; Self Reflection participants revised none (PDF p. 6, Section 4.1.2). These are component results of the combined edit outcome; counts of people who revised ideas are not arm sample sizes.

contrasts.reported: Kruskal-Wallis H(2) = 12.42, p = .002, epsilon^2 = .28. Interactive Engagement M = 1.93, SD = 0.96 vs Self Reflection M = 0.53, SD = 0.92: p_adj = .002, Hedges' g = 1.45. Stepwise Guidance M = 1.60, SD = 1.24 vs Self Reflection: p_adj = .031, g = 0.95. Stepwise Guidance vs Interactive Engagement not significant.

outcomes.name: Self-rated reconsideration ("To what extent did the activity prompt you to reconsider what makes a design effective for this challenge?")
outcomes.question: none

contrasts.reported: H(2) = 8.30, p = .016, epsilon^2 = .19. Interactive Engagement M = 5.47, SD = 1.252 vs Self Reflection M = 4.00, SD = 1.77: p_adj = .030, g = 0.93. Stepwise Guidance M = 5.47, SD = 1.246 vs Self Reflection: p_adj = .048, g = 0.93.

outcomes.name: Total ideas in the second iteration
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Total number of idea units in each participant's second-iteration proposal. Figure 2, left panel, prints rounded arm means and draws confidence intervals without numeric limits. The adjacent text supplies a more precise mean and SD only for Self Reflection (PDF p. 5, Section 4.1). The second iteration follows the intervention in the same session; removal of AI-generated sticky notes is not reported (PDF p. 4, Section 3.3.2).

contrasts.reported: Figure 2 second-round bar labels: Self Reflection 8.3, Stepwise Guidance 6.7, Interactive Engagement 6.7. Adjacent text: Self Reflection M = 8.33, SD = 2.06. Stepwise Guidance SD = null (not reported); Interactive Engagement SD = null (not reported). No between-arm test of second-iteration total idea counts is reported.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5, Section 4.1 and Figure 2, left panel (bar labels visually verified)

outcomes.name: Total ideas changed between iterations
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Overall number of ideas added, edited, or deleted between the two proposal iterations (PDF p. 4, Section 3.3.3; p. 5, Section 4.1 and Figure 2, right panel). The reported test is an omnibus comparison across all conditions; no pairwise test is given for this total.

contrasts.reported: Interactive Engagement M = 3.47, SD = 1.51; omnibus H(2) = 1.20, p = .548. Self Reflection total-change M = null, SD = null; Stepwise Guidance total-change M = null, SD = null (not printed; Figure 2 shows component segments).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5, Section 4.1, paragraph immediately below Figure 2

outcomes.name: Ideas deleted between iterations
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Deletion of idea units from the first proposal iteration, coded from proposals and verbal evidence (PDF p. 4, Section 3.3.3; p. 5, Section 3.4.1). Section 4.1.3 reports group totals and counts of participants who deleted ideas; these are not arm sample sizes. Figure 3 shows deletion counts by participant (PDF pp. 5-6).

contrasts.reported: Three Interactive Engagement participants deleted four ideas in total; two Stepwise Guidance participants deleted three ideas in total; no deletions occurred in Self Reflection. No inferential test of deletion differences is reported.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6, Section 4.1.3; Figure 3 on p. 5

eligibility.reason: Students were randomly assigned to an AI-agent arm or two non-AI arms, satisfying criterion 1 (PDF p. 4, Section 3.3.2). The main study analyzed 45 people, with 45 design proposals and 90 iterations coded, so criterion 2 is not met (PDF p. 4, Section 3.3.2; p. 5, Sections 3.4-3.4.1). Distinct ideas added to participants' proposals were counted using proposal coding, think-aloud evidence, and walkthroughs (PDF p. 4, Section 3.3.3; p. 5, Sections 3.4.1 and 4.1.1). This is output-scored fluency measured by category_count under creativity-codebook.md, Section 6, and satisfies criterion 3 without a separate creativity or novelty rating. Core remains no solely because the main study has fewer than 50 people. It is a small randomized experiment for the screening report and two-screener review, with context_class = none (creativity-codebook.md, Section 3). The agent feedback occurred between iterations; the paper does not state that its generated sticky notes were removed, so phase order alone does not establish an unassisted after_ai outcome (PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1 and 3.3.2).

one_line_finding: Among 45 design students, the AI-agent arm edited more of its ideas than the self-reflection arm (M = 1.93 vs 0.53, p_adj = .002, g = 1.45; pp. 5-6) but did not add significantly more ideas (M = 1.27 vs 2.13, p_adj = .446; p. 5), and no creativity rating of the proposals was made.

applied.quote: We define idea addition as participants adding ideas in the second iteration that are different from the ideas in their first iteration.
